questions.title: Why is attention still bottlenecked by softmax if the paper says matrix multiplication has much higher throughput?
questions.question_body: In FlashAttention-3, the authors say that on H100 the FP16 matmul throughput is extremely high, while special functions like exponentials have much lower throughput. They even estimate that for attention with head dimension 128, the exponential part of softmax can take about 50% of the cycles relative to matmul. I am confused because I thought attention was dominated by the two GEMMs, namely $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top$ and $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}$. If GEMMs are so much more expensive in FLOPs, why does softmax become such a serious bottleneck? Is the point that wall-clock time is determined by hardware throughput rather than just operation count?

questions.title: What exactly is the 'local softmax' trick that lets FlashAttention avoid materializing $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{P}$?
questions.question_body: I understand standard attention as computing $\mathbf{S} = \alpha \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top$, then $\mathbf{P} = \mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{S})$, then $\mathbf{O} = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}$. The paper says FlashAttention uses a blockwise or local softmax reduction so that $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{P}$ do not need to be written to HBM. But in the pseudocode, it keeps running values $m_i$, $\ell_i$, and rescales $\mathbf{O}_i$ each iteration. I do not see why this gives the same result as full row-wise softmax over the entire sequence. Could someone explain the algebra behind how the running row max and running normalization recover the exact attention output?

questions.title: Why does FlashAttention-3 split warps into producer and consumer roles instead of letting every warp do both loading and compute?
questions.question_body: The paper emphasizes 'warp-specialization' where some warps only issue TMA loads and others only issue WGMMA and softmax-related computation. I am confused why this is better than a more symmetric design where each warp loads its own data and computes on it. Is the main benefit reduced instruction scheduling complexity, better overlap of asynchronous units, better register allocation through `setmaxnreg`, or something else? I am trying to understand what problem warp-specialization solves that FlashAttention-2 could not.

questions.title: How can softmax be overlapped with GEMM if softmax depends on the output of $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top$?
questions.question_body: The paper says one of the main ideas is to 'hide softmax under asynchronous block-wise GEMMs'. But softmax on block $j$ needs the scores $\mathbf{S}_i^{(j)} = \mathbf{Q}_i\mathbf{K}_j^\top$, so I would think the first GEMM must fully finish before softmax can even start. Then the second GEMM $\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}_i^{(j)}\mathbf{V}_j$ must wait for softmax. So this looks sequential to me. In Algorithm 2, they seem to break the dependency by pipelining across iterations using $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{cur}}$ and $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{next}}$. Could someone explain carefully which dependencies remain and which ones are avoided by the 2-stage pipeline?

questions.title: What does 'commit but do not wait' mean for WGMMA, and why is that useful here?
questions.question_body: In the consumer algorithm, the paper repeatedly says to issue a WGMMA, then 'commit but do not wait'. Later it explicitly waits for the result before using it. I think the idea is that WGMMA is asynchronous on Hopper, but I am not sure what state the computation is in after 'commit'. Does this mean the instruction has been launched to Tensor Cores but the CUDA cores can continue executing unrelated instructions? If so, what kinds of operations are actually safe to overlap before the later wait, and how does the kernel avoid reading incomplete accumulator values?

questions.title: Why does pingpong scheduling need two warpgroups and explicit barriers if the hardware is already asynchronous?
questions.question_body: The paper describes 'pingpong scheduling' where warpgroup 1 performs GEMMs while warpgroup 2 performs softmax, then they swap roles. I am confused why this requires carefully ordered barriers such as `bar.sync`. If WGMMA and TMA are already asynchronous, shouldn't the hardware naturally overlap whatever is ready? Is the point that without barriers, the compiler or scheduler might issue both warpgroups' GEMMs first and postpone the non-GEMM softmax work, which would underutilize special-function units? I would like to understand what is enforced by pingpong scheduling that would not happen automatically.

questions.title: Why are the buffer stages for $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{V}$ released at different times in the pipelined algorithm?
questions.question_body: In the simpler algorithm, each iteration loads $\mathbf{K}_j$ and $\mathbf{V}_j$ into the same circular shared-memory pipeline stage and later releases that stage. But in the 2-stage algorithm, the code releases the stage for $\mathbf{K}_j$ and the stage for $\mathbf{V}_{j-1}$ separately. I am getting lost in the lifetime of each tile. Is this because $\mathbf{K}_j$ is only needed for the first GEMM of iteration $j$, while $\mathbf{V}_{j-1}$ is still needed later for the second GEMM? A timeline-style explanation of when each tile can be safely overwritten would help.

questions.title: Why does the 2-stage pipeline increase register pressure by roughly one extra $\mathbf{S}$ tile?
questions.question_body: The paper says the extra buffering required by the 2-stage pipeline means keeping an additional score tile like $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{next}}$ in registers, with extra storage on the order of $B_r \times B_c \times \mathrm{sizeof}(\mathrm{float})$ per threadblock. I do not fully understand where this quantity comes from. Is it because while softmax is consuming the current scores, the next scores from $\mathbf{Q}_i\mathbf{K}_j^\top$ have already been produced and must remain live until the wait finishes? Also, are these accumulators really all stored in registers rather than shared memory?

questions.title: Why does FP8 WGMMA only supporting k-major operands create a special problem for attention?
questions.question_body: The paper states that for FP16 WGMMA, both mn-major and k-major shared-memory layouts are allowed, but for FP8 WGMMA only k-major is supported. I am struggling to connect this hardware detail to the attention algorithm. In particular, the authors say this causes trouble for the second GEMM involving $\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}\mathbf{V}$. Is the issue that $\mathbf{V}$ is normally stored contiguous in the head-dimension direction, while the FP8 Tensor Core expects the shared-memory tile in the opposite contiguity? If so, why does this matter specifically when trying to fuse the two GEMMs in one kernel?

questions.title: Why does FlashAttention-3 transpose $\mathbf{V}$ tiles inside the kernel instead of transposing $\mathbf{V}$ once in global memory?
questions.question_body: For the FP8 path, the paper says there are two options: transpose $\mathbf{V}$ in global memory before attention, or load a tile and transpose it inside the kernel using LDSM and STSM. They choose the in-kernel transpose. I understand that a separate preprocessing transpose kernel would add bandwidth cost, but I am still unsure why that cost is large enough to dominate, especially if the transpose could be reused across multiple heads or layers. Is the main reason that attention during inference is memory-bound, so an extra read/write of all of $\mathbf{V}$ is too expensive compared to doing a tile-local shared-memory transpose on the fly?

questions.title: How does the register-byte permutation after the first FP8 WGMMA still produce the correct $\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}\mathbf{V}$ result?
questions.question_body: One of the most confusing parts for me is the FP8 layout fix. The paper says the FP32 accumulator layout produced by the first FP8 WGMMA does not match the layout expected for operand A of the second FP8 WGMMA, so they use byte-permute instructions to reorder the accumulator entries. They then say this logically permutes columns of the $\mathbf{P}$ tile, and they compensate by writing out a matching row permutation of the $\mathbf{V}$ tile during the in-kernel transpose. I think this means they are effectively multiplying $(\mathbf{P} \Pi)(\Pi^\top \mathbf{V})$ for some permutation matrix $\Pi$, which equals $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}$. Is that the right interpretation, or am I misunderstanding what is being permuted?

questions.title: Why does multiplying both $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{K}$ by an orthogonal matrix not change attention, and why is $\mathbf{V}$ left alone?
questions.question_body: The paper uses 'incoherent processing' by multiplying $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{K}$ with a random orthogonal matrix $\mathbf{M}$ before FP8 quantization, arguing that this spreads out outliers and reduces quantization error. They state that $(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{M})(\mathbf{K}\mathbf{M})^\top = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top$ because $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{M}^\top = I$. I follow that algebra, but I am not sure how this interacts with the scaling factor and the later multiplication by $\mathbf{V}$. Why is it enough to transform only $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{K}$, and not $\mathbf{V}$ as well? Also, does this preserve attention exactly before quantization and only change the quantization error profile?

questions.title: Why does block quantization have 'no computation cost' in this algorithm?
questions.question_body: The FP8 section says block quantization can be fused with an operation before attention, and that FlashAttention-3 can 'scale each block of $\mathbf{S}$ to account for this block quantization at no computation cost'. I do not see why the cost is effectively zero. If each block of $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{K}$ has its own scale, shouldn't the score block $\mathbf{S}_{ij}$ need to be multiplied by a corresponding factor such as $s_{Q,i} s_{K,j}$ before softmax? Is the claim simply that these multiplications are negligible compared to GEMMs, or is the scaling folded into existing instructions so no extra instructions are needed?

questions.title: Why is the backward-pass FLOP count estimated as $2.5$ times the forward-pass FLOPs?
questions.question_body: In the benchmarking section, the paper says forward FLOPs are computed as $4 \cdot \mathrm{seqlen}^2 \cdot \mathrm{head\ dimension} \cdot \mathrm{number\ of\ heads}$, and the backward pass is estimated as $2.5$ times the forward pass because there are 5 matmuls in backward versus 2 in forward due to recomputation. I can see from the equations that backward uses $\mathbf{P}^\top \mathbf{dO}$, $\mathbf{dO}\mathbf{V}^\top$, $\mathbf{dS}\mathbf{K}$, and $\mathbf{dS}^\top\mathbf{Q}$, but that is only 4 matmuls unless I am missing one. Which operation is being counted as the fifth matmul, and how exactly does recomputation enter this accounting?

questions.title: Why can FP8 FlashAttention-3 be slower than FP16 in some cases even though FP8 Tensor Cores have higher peak throughput?
questions.question_body: The paper reports nearly double measured throughput with FP8 WGMMA, but also says that for some settings, especially small sequence length or causal masking, FP8 FlashAttention-3 is only competitive with cuDNN and may lag behind. I am confused because I expected FP8 to be strictly faster than FP16 if the Tensor Core throughput is higher. Is the bottleneck shifting away from GEMM to softmax, transposes, layout conversions, or load balancing overhead? The discussion also mentions that the FP8 kernel does not yet use a persistent kernel design. I would appreciate a clearer explanation of why higher arithmetic peak does not automatically translate into end-to-end attention speedup.
